Mr. Speaker, I should like as a matter of privilege to explain at once to the house that, in reviewing the Hansard report of the answer I gave on Friday to a question by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) with regard to the shipments of arms or equipment from Canada, I found my words were not as precise as they should have been.
I said that "at the present time we are as much concerned about the situation in the Middle East as is any hon. member of the house, and that there will be no shipments pending the debate on the matter in the House of Commons." The whole discussion had arisen, in fact, out of the concern about the situation in the Middle East, and I intended my words about shipments to refer to that area which I had just mentioned, and I believe everyone understood that they did refer to that area.
However, when I saw the transcript, it seemed to me the words about shipments might be misunderstood and perhaps taken to mean there would be no shipments to any country, including our North Atlantic allies, and I therefore inserted after the word "shipments" the words "for that area", and I wanted to take this first opportunity to explain to the house that I had done so to remove any possibility of misinterpretation of the statement elsewhere or even here in parliament.

On Thursday last, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition asked me a supplementary question following a question which he had asked of my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs with respect to the ability of the Harvard trainer to carry weapons. -have any steps been taken to ensure that military weapons are not provided for the Harvard trainers being shipped to Egypt?

Last week, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Royal asked if it is the intention of the government to move the fisheries research station from St. Andrews, N.B., to Halifax, N.S.
Inquiries of the Ministry
The answer is no. Since 1944 this station has grown from a staff of 10 full-time and 7 seasonal employees to 96 full-time and 29 seasonal employees. St. Andrews is the ideal location for the biological station serving the maritime provinces, since it is situated in the heart of most of the fisheries.
One or two maritime fisheries however are not centred around St. Andrews and so for some years we have stationed employees at Ellerslie, P.E.I., and Shippigan, N.B., for oyster studies, and at Chatham, N.B., for smelt studies.
The fisheries research board has now recommended establishing two other small detachments at Halifax to be closer to their work.
The international commission for the northwest Atlantic fisheries has established its headquarters at Dalhousie University, Halifax. Halifax is also the centre of our deep-sea trawler fleet and so it is felt that the section studying groundfish should be stationed there to carry out our share of research work for the commission.
The Royal Canadian Navy and the Department of Fisheries have a joint program of oceanographic studies. Since the navy provides personnel and vessels from their Halifax base, the work will be better carried out if the fisheries scientists are stationed at Halifax.
The total personnel affected is about 20. The move will be carried out gradually over the next two years to avoid inconvenience to the employees affected. The move will also relieve the present overcrowding at St. Andrews station.

Mr. Speaker, one of the most welcome proposals in the speech from the throne is the plan to speed up the completion of the trans-Canada highway. The Canadian public has become very impatient in the last few years with the seemingly endless delays in getting our first trans-Canada highway completed from coast to coast. It has been said very often that we seem to have lost the art of spanning our continent in spite of our tremendous advances in recent years in technological knowledge. About half a century ago, with far less population and with far less material resources than we have today, we had built two or three transcontinental railways. However, under this new proposal it is hoped that the trans-Canada highway can be completed finally on the new schedule.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that some people have been dragging their feet on this trans-Canada highway scheme. Otherwise it would have been completed long ago. What we need, I believe, is a national highway program similar to the program which exists in the 6750&-26
The Address-Mr. Hanna United States. I think we should already be planning for trans-Canada highway No. 2 and hon. members will not be surprised, I am sure, if I suggest it should go through the centre of the prairie provinces by way of Edmonton and the Yellowhead pass and on to the Pacific coast.
I also think we need more highways into northern Canada to speed up development there. Already a start has been made by building the Mackenzie highway through northern Alberta into the Northwest Territories, but I believe additional roads are needed in the Northwest Territories to speed up and encourage development in that part of the country. I am also convinced, Mr. Speaker, that we badly need a new railway line to tap the great resources of the Northwest Territories. It seems to me that such a railway should be made a continuation of the railway lines that exist already in northern Alberta for those railways extend further north than do any other railways in that part of the country at the present time.
More specifically, I believe that Canadian National Railways should extend its line northward from Waterways, Alberta, to Pine Point on Great Slave lake. I hope that the government will consider some form of financial assistance to encourage such extension being made, similar to the financial assistance granted to the Pacific Great Eastern Railway in British Columbia.
I have suggested the extension of both highways and railways into the north. These facilities would not necessarily be in competition one with the other. I believe that both are needed and that the one would complement the other.
I am sure that all hon. members of this house were gratified to hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) say a few days ago that the representations of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind and the Canadian Council of the Blind were receiving his careful consideration. These representations ask for a basic allowance for all blind persons without any means test. I am reliably informed that Australia and Denmark, and possibly other countries, already have such a provision in their social welfare legislation and I believe that Canada should be kept in the forefront with our excellent Liberal social security program.
There is meeting today in Ottawa a dominion-provincial conference to study proposals for a national health insurance program. We all hope that that conference will be a success and that out of it will come definite proposals for a national health insurance plan.
We have all noted with a great deal of satisfaction that our gross national product

I point out to these new Liberal members what happened last year when this same minister laid down the party line, when he said he had to have his full wartime powers under the Defence Production Act on a permanent basis. 1 point out to them what happened to the handful of Liberal members who were rash enough to support him on the

floor of the house. The only one who derived any benefit from it was the former member for Spadina, who, of course, found a haven in the Senate.
The Prime Minister also followed this party line laid down by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He followed it, for example, for weeks after the debate in the house began, telling us the minister simply had to have these powers or the government of Canada could not go on. Then, once he had the minister away on a fishing trip in New Brunswick, the Prime Minister ran up the white flag and made the most abject surrender to the official opposition that has been made since confederation. Of course, that only happened because he as Prime Minister had failed miserably to give leadership on this question. He knew from the start that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and of Defence Production was wrong and knew that action should have been taken to stop that minister earlier, but did nothing until weeks of debate had gone on.
If the advice of the Minister of Trade and Commerce is to be taken and the Liberal party members in this house are to toe the party line-and how they can do it more than they have been in the past I find it hard to imagine-the result will be that private members on the government side of the house will be gagged. That position has been the weakest feature of this parliament since it was elected two years ago.
Today I intend to deal with four subjects which did not find a place in the speech from the throne. That means, I suggest, that the government places very little importance on these particular subjects.
First of all, the speech forecast no legislation whatever for the veterans of Canada. Evidently the government has no intention of amending the existing veterans legislation, of introducing any additional measures to help the veterans of this country, or of setting up a committee on veterans affairs- either a standing committee, as so many of us have requested for years, or a special sessional committee.
In fact, the government's attitude is even more reprehensible in that the department now has only a half-time minister. That shows again the failure of the Prime Minister of this country to give leadership. He has allowed this session to commence without the veterans of Canada having a full-time minister to look after the problems which are of concern to them. It shows also the Prime Minister's low estimate of the ability of his parliamentary assistants. He has a great number of them ready, anxious and willing to become ministers, and yet apparently not one of them is suitable to be made 67509-26i
The Address-Mr. Green the minister of veterans affairs or the postmaster general. It shows also his low estimate of the private members on the government side of the house. There are 170 Liberal members, but apparently among all the private members there is not one fit to take over one of these portfolios. But far more serious than that is this fact, that the failure to have a full-time minister of veterans affairs is unfair to the veterans of Canada. It is an insult to those veterans.
There are certain necessary changes that should be made in veterans legislation. I have not the time today to list them in detail, but I shall point out three or four. For example, there is a deadline in the Pension Act after which a veteran who marries cannot receive any payment for his wife, and if he dies his widow cannot receive a pension. That deadline is set at May 1, 1954. It should be advanced or removed altogether. I cannot see any reason why there should be such a deadline. It was written into the legislation in the first place to protect the veteran from deathbed marriages. In the United States there had been cases of young women marrying extremely old veterans simply to get a pension. In Canada previous governments have felt that such a thing should be prevented and hence the deadline. But there is no deadline for veterans of the second world war and there is no deadline under the War Veterans Allowance Act; also there is a wide discretion in the pension commission to deal with each application. I think the time has come to remove this deadline entirely.
Then the ceiling for the war veterans allowance should be raised. That question was debated at some length during the last session. I believe the time has now come when the permissive income should be increased to $1,200 for the single veteran and $2,000 for the married veteran as requested by the Canadian Legion. If that were done, recipients of war veterans allowance would be able to draw the full amount of old age security when they reach 70 years of age. That is something they are not able to do today.
Another improvement which should be made at this session is that provision should be made for the payment of war veterans allowance to veterans who are compelled to live beyond the borders of Canada for reasons of health. The other day I had an example of a veteran who was obliged to go to Mexico in order to stay alive. At the present time he can stay there only three months without losing his war veterans allowance. The result is that he must come back to Canada to die. I think that is an unfair situation. The same thing applies, of course, with regard to old

The Address-Mr. Green age security. It should not be beyond the ability of this parliament to frame some provision that will enable people to go outside of Canada, if they must do so in order to stay alive. Some provision should1 be made to enable them to do so and still draw these allowances.
Also provision should be made for the widow of an Imperial veteran where that veteran came to Canada before the year 1935; at the present time, unless her husband was in Canada for 20 years, she cannot qualify. That means that if he died after he had been here for 19J years, his widow has no eligibility. In addition, the Canadian Legion made various recommendations to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and other members of the cabinet last fall for amendments to the pension act and also for further amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. These matters should be considered by this house during the present session.
I urge the Prime Minister to appoint a separate Minister of Veterans Affairs without further delay, also that he arrange for the consideration of these points that I have enumerated, and for the appointment of a committee on veterans affairs, preferably a standing committee.
The second subject which is not mentioned in the speech from the throne is the International River Improvements Act which was passed by this house last year and which was designed to meet a situation that had arisen on the Columbia river system in British Columbia. Hon. members will recall that there were several lengthy debates on this question. The bill was considered by the standing committee on external affairs. There was a great deal of publicity about the matter for many months and there was almost a civil war between the federal government and the government of British Columbia. In the final analysis, this particular bill was passed. Yet today, in 1956, it seems to have been forgotten. Apparently it has been put on the shelf by the government along with many other policies such as, should I say, that on health insurance.
I should like to outline the reasons for this legislation and the result. For 10 years, ever since 1945, joint investigations had been carried on in the Columbia river basin by dominion and provincial engineers. Then late in 1954 the British Columbia government proposed to make a deal with a United States company known as the Kaiser Aluminum and Chemical Corporation under which a dam would be constructed at the foot of the Arrow lakes. The federal government took a dim view of that proposal on the ground that such a dam would prevent the full


utilization of the Columbia river system in Canada. I think the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) will agree that that was the basis for the dispute between the two governments. Eventually this International River Improvements Act was passed. It established a licensing control by the dominion over the improvements on all international rivers, having in mind primarily the Columbia river.
I have here a report, tabled by the minister a few days ago, showing operations under this act up to the end of December, 1955. The report sums up the purpose of the act very well in these words:
This act provides for the licensing of international river improvements to ensure that the water resources of Canada are developed and utilized in the national interest.
I think that is a good description of the purpose of the act. The report goes on to show that no applications whatever for licences were received during the year.

Before governments can discuss the matter, certainly as far as we are concerned we want it to be discussed by the persons whom we consider to be the experts in the matter on both sides of the border.
There were further questions and answers to the same effect. I notice that in the regulations which have come out there is a provision that an applicant for a licence must give details of any agreement if it is intended to sell outside of Canada any part of the Canadian share of downstream power resulting from the proposed international river improvement. Although that has been put into the regulations, apparently nothing has been done towards negotiating any treaty with the United States concerning these downstream benefits. One of the federal government's main complaints against the British Columbia government last year was that it had attempted to make a deal which covered in part downstream benefits before a treaty had been negotiated, and yet we find this provision written into the regulations under the act.
In October I had the good fortune to meet Senator Richard L. Neuberger of Oregon when he was in Nelson while on a tour of the Kootenay district as a representative of the committee on interior and insular affairs of the United States Senate. He had been sent out by the chairman of that committee to inquire, on behalf of the committee, into the problem concerning the future development of the Columbia river in Canada. Our own minister has been kind enough to give me a copy of the senator's report, and I received one as well from the senator himself. It is very helpful in showing just what the position is concerning downstream benefits.
The senator, by the way, took a very fair attitude on this whole question. He was going around inviting representations from
The Address-Mr. Green people in the district and listening to their views. I thought he had a very statesmanlike approach to the whole question and his report is an excellent one. He makes several recommendations to his Senate committee, and I propose to quote two of the recommendations. The introduction to his recommendations is as follows:
As a result of my own study trip on behalf of the committee, I recommend that the Senate committee on interior and insular affairs schedule public hearings at the earliest possible time to inquire into the status of plans and negotiations for the development of the upper Columbia river to the mutual benefit of the United States and Canada.
On the basis of the report which follows, I also make these substantive recommendations for consideration by the committee at such hearings:
1. That responsibility within the United States government for these important negotiations be raised from the level of a purely advisory committee like the United States section of the international joint commission and be explicitly assumed by the policymaking executive departments themselves.
I believe that recommendation should be put into effect in Canada. It is obvious that the chairman of the United States section of the commission is against downstream benefits, and I feel it is a waste of time to have the commission study this matter. It must be settled between the two governments.
The senator adds this further recommendation:
6. That this committee express its firm intent that, in our negotiations with Canada, no effort be spared to arrive at the best possible program for the development of the upper Columbia riverbeginning now with the construction of the Libby and Mica projects-so as to maximize the mutual benefits to both countries which share this unique resource. Such a determined and constructive effort must give frank and open-minded consideration to the fair allocation of upstream costs and downstream benefits attributable to upstream storage-including possible sharing of benefits in generated electric power.
Now, as I understand it, that is what the Canadian government says. The senator also has this paragraph which I think is of great importance:
Failure to reach agreement on a mutually beneficial program for developing the Columbia river would threaten the gravest crisis in modem U.S.-Canadian relations, as well as incalculable economic loss to both countries. Agreement and execution of such a program, on the other hand, can assure economic progress for a generation to come for the Pacific northwest in both countries, and can make a material contribution to the industrial and defensive strength of the North American continent and the western alliance.
I do suggest to our own minister that the Canadian government take steps at once to initiate negotiations for a treaty with the United States covering downstream benefits.

Mr. Speaker, along with many previous speakers I wish to pay tribute to the mover (Mrs. Shipley) and seconder (Mr. Laflamme) of the motion to adopt the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
The hon. lady from Timiskaming, with her usual direct and charming manner, brought distinction to her sex, her constituency and herself by the able manner in which she proposed the motion we are now debating. She spoke with clarity and authority of the affairs of her constituency. Therefore, we who are associated with her as representatives of similar constituencies in northern Ontario are proud to take our stand with her as supporters of this government. My congratulations are also extended to the hon. member for Bellechasse on his contribution.
I have the honour to represent the constituency of Sudbury. When the new constituency of Nickel Belt was created in the redistribution of 1953 by absorbing the suburban portion of the old constituency of Sudbury, the urban portion which I represent remained under the name Sudbury. Owing to the vast increase in population we now have two ridings instead of one, Nickel Belt being so ably represented by my genial colleague on the government side of the house.
We have a very cosmopolitan population comprising dozens of nationalities, which makes it a melting pot in the true sense of the word. As an example, in the last year only, at three sittings in the judge's chambers over 600 individuals have received their Canadian naturalization papers. This is indeed a fine record, and these new citizens are taking their place with us to plan and form a strong community and a prosperous Canada.
Most of the rapid expansion and development in our area is due to the gigantic industrial influence exerted by the International

Nickel Company which operates six mines and two smelters in the immediate district. The discovery of nickel occurred in 1885 when the railway was being constructed through our district. During rock cut blasting the metals of copper and nickel were uncovered and over the years this metal discovery has grown in leaps and bounds to the immense position in the industrial field it now enjoys. Ninety per cent of the world's supply of nickel is produced in the Sudbury area, with copper second in importance. Other metals in impressive amounts recovered in the smelting process are platinum, palladium, rhodium, ruthenium, gold, silver, cobalt, selenium, tellurium and sulphur and, of course, sulphuric acid. Now iron ore is soon to be added to this group of metals. The company has just completed the construction of an iron smelter at a cost of $19 million, and when all three units are in production will have an annual output of one million tons.
The International Nickel Company has an underground production of 44,000 tons per mine operating day and last year mined 14,468,000 tons. The proven ore reserves stand at 261 million tons, which would indicate continued prosperity for this region for many years. The figures, et cetera, to which I have referred, apply as well to the Falcon-bridge Nickel Mines, also in our area, but to a much smaller degree. As an example, the International Nickel Company employs 16,000 in our area and Falconbridge approximately 3,000.
I have described the great development and continued growth in industrial might of the Sudbury district to emphasize the contribution my district makes to our peacetime economy and to our security in time of war. This is indeed a billion dollar industry. Because a large proportion of the products are exported, chiefly to the United States, the stabilizing effect on our currency and the maintenance of the balance of trade between our two countries can be readily realized.
I should like for a few minutes to comment on some of the results of good legislation by this government, which has been of great benefit to my riding and which has added to our prosperity and economic structure. We have the fortunate distinction of being at the northern junction of two trans-Canada highways. The present one from Ottawa runs west to join the one running through the central part of the province, turning north at Parry Sound and meeting the present highway at Sudbury. It then continues west as one to terminate eventually at the Pacific coast. This, in itself, certainly puts Sudbury

on the main line for motor transportation adding to the main line of the C.P.R. which has served us for so many years.
"Now we are working on the pipe line", as it has been so ably put. Because northern Ontario has been mentioned so often in the construction of the trans-Canada pipe line, it would be of value to estimate what an advantage it would be to us in Sudbury and in the north generally. The mechanics of this service were very thoroughly explained a few days ago by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Carrick), so no further enlightenment seems to be necessary. Suffice it to say that we will welcome this service and use it to the best of our ability both in domestic and industrial consumption. I have been led to believe, though not by any authority, that should the International Nickel Company be convinced that this type of fuel would be more economical than that in use at present they would convert their furnaces to its use. If such a conversion should be made and the company use gas instead of coal or electricity for their blast furnaces, it is estimated that Inco would use more gas as fuel than would be consumed by any of the large cities of Canada for their many needs.
The hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) visited our city last summer and officially opened our airport. This has been a real contribution by the T.C.A. to link us more quickly with the rest of the world, and I am glad to report it has enjoyed satisfactory traffic on this feeder line. As everyone is becoming more air conscious every day, we are indeed proud to have been included in this expansion program. The airstrip is of standard length so I hope soon we will be serviced with the larger aircraft and find ourselves on the main east-west flight across Canada.
We are well serviced with television. The Sudbury privately-owned television station was the first in Canada to be granted a licence and is quite capably performing its public relations and supplying good informative and entertaining programs. We are authoritatively advised that we will be served this fall by the microwave hook-up which will be a welcome addition and carry live programs to us. All this will add to the pleasure of our leisure time and be of value to the cultural life of the community.
I would like to bring to the attention of hon. members that the only bottleneck in the rapid growth and development of our district is the service of our railways. Of course we are fully aware that the C.P.R. was located in Sudbury before this city was more than a village, but at the present time their station and yards have become wholly outdated and
The Address-Mr. Knowles there seems to be no evidence of any attempt to cope with the problems consequent upon the advance of the city. As it stands now, the city is cut in half with the main line and switching tracks and the centre of the city tied up in vacant and undeveloped land which could be quickly absorbed for industrial or residential sites.
The yards are so inadequate that trains have to be held out on the main line and prevented from entering the yards by the severe congestion confronting them. Passengers entraining during the rush hours must cross through trains to board others. This is most unsatisfactory. At least two main crossings are almost continuously blocked by trains switching for nearly 24 hours a day, and vehicular traffic is tied up as a result.
It is quite evident the C.P.R. enjoys the major amount of traffic and resulting revenue in our city and is also aware of the difficulty they will have in attempting to expand their service owing to being hemmed in by the city being built all around them.
Under these conditions it is unbelievable that the C.N.R. has made no effort to assist in meeting the traffic demand and consider making Sudbury a competitive point by increasing their service. Surely for the assistance of the Sudbury area the C.N.R. can make an immediate investigation and take action to help remedy this chaotic and decadent condition. The citizens of Sudbury are demanding a solution for this problem and it is for this reason I am making this appeal to the hon. minister who, I hope, will bring this state of affairs in Sudbury to the attention of the president of the C.N.R.
In conclusion I want to congratulate the government on many acts that have helped our area. A few may be mentioned: the Lome street subway which received considerable federal aid; the new federal building about to be constructed to house all federal departments; the R.C.A.F. radar station which is not too far from our city; and the air services, referred to earlier, made possible by the construction of a new airport.

Mr. Speaker, there is being held in Ottawa today one of the most important conferences that has been held for a long time. I refer to the conference being attended by the Minister of National Defence and Welfare (Mr. Martin) along with his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), and their opposite numbers representing the ten provincial governments. As all hon. members are aware, the purpose of this conference is to study the question of health insurance. I shall not take any time to dwell upon the

The Address-Mr. Knowles many years that it has taken to reach the point where it begins to look as though something may be done, but I want to say that I chose deliberately to speak today in order that I might draw to the attention of the federal government the fact that of the groups represented at this conference its part is the most important of all.
We all recognize the importance of federal-provincial co-operation in the field of health insurance; we all recognize the important part that must be played by the provinces and by authorities even more local than the provinces; we all recognize the importance of the part played by the medical profession; but the key to any successful health insurance program lies in the method by which such a program is to be financed.
When it comes to the successful financing of a program of the proportions of a national health insurance scheme no local, voluntary or provincial authority has the financial capacity to deal with it satisfactorily. The only body in this country that has the financial capacity to deal with this problem is the federal government.
There are those who still contend that it would be best to leave as much of this as possible to voluntary agencies such as the Blue Cross, Blue Shield and similar organizations, and there are also those who still want to leave the major responsibility for health insurance to the provinces. When one deals with this matter he is not dealing in the realm of theory. The fact is that the experiences of some of the provinces and of voluntary organizations have made it clear that they cannot put health insurance on a financial basis that will be satisfactory, and by satisfactory I mean one that will get health services to the Canadian people according to their need for such services rather than according to their individual financial capacity.
Only within the last little while changes have been made in the rates both of the Blue Cross and the Blue Shield in my province of Manitoba which stress the point that I am making. In the case of the Blue Cross, which we know as the Manitoba hospital services association, whilst there has been no change in the basic rates for some considerable time, a constant change is going on in that groups of people insured under that plan are one by one being put into a category that requires payment of a certain percentage of one's hospital bill. The basis upon which certain groups are being put into that category is that in the view of the Manitoba Blue Cross they are poor insurance risks.

Similarly, the Manitoba medical service, just a short while ago, announced-not publicly, but by informing those affected-that groups of its subscribers who from experience have been found to be poor risks, in the sense that they need more medical care than others, are being put on a higher rate than those who experience has shown do not require quite so much medical attention. In other words, these voluntary organizations, which in filling the gap left by the federal government have done a good job, nevertheless admit that the only way they can carry on is by imposing the cost of hospitalization and of medical services, so far as possible, on the people who actually get that hospitalization or those medical services. This is not insurance at all; insurance calls for spreading the cost over a larger group than those actually hospitalized or given treatment.
There was a day when it was regarded as radical to advocate that everyone should receive education, that education should not be limited to those who could afford to pay for it. There are still some who think that that principle is radical when applied to hospital and medical services. But the fact is that our society has moved on a great deal, and most people who do any thinking at all about this matter today realize that medical matters are of social concern and that our people should get the hospitalization and medical services they require, because they need them and not because of the length of their purses.
I submit that, because the voluntary agencies are finding that they have no alternative but to charge on a flat rate or premium basis, or to charge on a basis where the cost gets back to the people who actually get those services, you are not by that means implementing the principle that health care should be made available to those who need it and that we should all pay for it according to our ability to pay. The only way in which that principle can be put into effect in this country is by the federal government providing the financial basis, and by making available out of general revenue the major portion of the cost of health services.
Therefore, important as is the place assumed at this conference today by the various provincial governments, I submit that the most important part will be that played by the federal government. I call upon the federal government not merely to look for the least common denominator, to sit back and hope that some arbitrary formula will not be met so that the blame for inaction can be put on the provinces, but rather I call upon the federal government to give leadership with respect to this most important

issue and to make a financial proposition to the provinces on the basis of the federal government's capacity for raising money according to the ability of the Canadian people to pay, so that we shall get a health insurance plan for Canadians that will really be a step forward.
It has been a pleasure during the course of this debate to hear many more hon. members speaking about health insurance than has been the case in former years. Of course, once it is mentioned in the speech from the throne-that happened many years ago when I first came here-that there is to be a conference of the various governments dealing with the matter, it becomes the thing to do. However, it is not good enough just to have a conference in session, just to have the notion that something will be done. The important thing is that health insurance get started in the right way. Thus a related reason for my urging the federal government to realize its importance at this conference, a related reason for my urging the federal government to give real leadership, is that I do not want to see health insurance programs in this country get off to a wrong start. I do not want them to get to a situation where we have to try to unscramble the omelet. Let us not run the risk of a hodgepodge that would not do the job. There is danger of that at the present time unless the federal government is willing to establish the basic principles of health insurance and lay them down in enabling legislation that will provide for proper health insurance right across this country.
We have at the present time hospital schemes in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and to some extent in Newfoundland. We have voluntary hospital schemes in most of the other provinces. We have the premier of Ontario indicating that, whether or not something is done at the federal level, there will be action in this field in the province of Ontario. No two of any of these schemes thus far are identical. My suspicion is that, if Ontario goes it alone apart from the federal government, its scheme will likewise be different from those in effect in the other provinces where a start has been made. Ontario with its greater wealth could do better perhaps than some of the other provinces, but even Ontario will face the same limitations. Because it does not have the same tax base that the federal government has, it will not be able to go all the way in implementing the principle that we should pay for health services according to our ability to pay and receive those services according to our need for them. That means financing those services mainly out of general revenues. I am satisfied that, if there is
The Address-Mr. Knowles not a national plan, if there is not a basic federal enabling act so that we get off to a good start, the day will come when we shall have to unscramble the omelet, when we shall have to undo the hodge-podge of the different kinds of schemes we have in the different provinces. Would it not be the part of wisdom and the part of statesmanship by this present government to avoid a hodgepodge, to avoid an unsatisfactory situation, by offering now to the provinces, this very day, the kind of legislation that will finance a health insurance scheme on a proper basis letting each province come in as it wishes, as was done with old age pensions and give us a chance to go forward step by step into a full-grown program rather than a hodgepodge that would have to be unscrambled?
I want to urge that there be no stumbling-blocks put in the way of a national health insurance program. We have had many of them across the years. Everyone knows that the latest formula is to the effect that the federal government will be prepared to assist in the financing of a health insurance plan in the provinces that wish it if a substantial majority of the provinces, representing a substantial majority of the people of Canada, indicate that they want it. I hope that formula will be met. I hope there will be six provinces-and surely that is a substantial majority of the provinces-indicating that they want health insurance. If Ontario is one of them, along with British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Newfoundland, and possibly one more, surely that adds up to a substantial majority of the population of this country. But even if the formula is not met in its exact detail, I suggest that the people of Canada will feel that once again they have been let down if for that reason no action is taken.
Across the years we have had the related question as to how an amendment could be made to the British North America Act. This discussion has been sidetracked into the question of how many provinces would have to agree before there could be an amendment of the British North America Act; and we have had discussions as to whether or not this was necessary, depending on whether the money collected for this purpose was collected by way of general taxation or by way of earmarked taxation. We have had the excuse that there were not enough hospital beds. We have been told to wait until the national health grants program resulted in more hospital beds and more facilities. Then, just when we thought we were making headway and just when we thought there was going to be a special committee of both houses of parliament to deal with this matter,
404	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Knowles in the same way that a special committee dealt with old age security, the international situation took a turn which enabled the government to say that defence commitments stood in the way of spending additional money on health services.
The Canadian people are conscious of this long list of excuses with which we have been confronted since 1919. They want action now. The eyes of Canada are on this conference that is taking place in Ottawa at the present time. Once again I urge the federal government to realize that its job is not just to sit there and find the least common denominator but that its job is to give leadership and to accept the fact that only the federal government can provide the financial base that will make it possible to provide health services to our people according to their need for these services, and let them be paid for by our people not according to the service individuals get but according to their ability to pay.
I wish also, Mr. Speaker, to urge that any health insurance plan worked out at the present time, in which the government must take the leading part, should include not just a minimum of services with the idea that they can be added to 10 years or 20 years from now but rather should include just as many services as possible. I am free to admit that maybe you cannot go the whole way at one fell swoop. The tragedy is that this program was not started a long time ago, at least as long ago as in the early 1940's, the first time it was mentioned in the speech from the throne. If we had only done that, by now we could be moving on to the addition of other services. But at least, Mr. Speaker, the initial stages should include diagnostic services, laboratory services and hospitalization.
I am disturbed by the comments from federal government sources which suggest that hospitalization is not very high on the list. It should be right up there in the first stage. From there on the program should be capable of being developed until it includes medical and dental services and even until it includes sickness benefits for the breadwinner when he is out of work, either in the health insurance program or in the unemployment insurance program.
This is an extremely important field of social security, Mr. Speaker. Its potentialities are immense for improving the health of our people, the morale of our people and their productivity, if you will.
I insist that the opportunity must not be muffed by politics being played at the conference today, by governments looking to next elections or what-have-you, but rather all those at the conference should take advantage of the tremendous amount of research 

and study that has been done in this field and should come up with a program that will really mean something for the Canadian people.
I know there are those who will raise the old question of cost. I also know that the cost of an adequate national health program is today immensely more than it would have been in 1945 at the time of the green book proposals. However, it is still true that any national health insurance program that provides health services to all our people is not going to involve the expenditure of a great deal of new money. For the most part it is a case of rechannelling moneys that are now being spent by various levels of government, by private and voluntary organizations, by philanthropic bodies and by individuals. It is difficult to ascertain just what proportion of the medical costs of Canada are being paid by these various levels. Research done on the matter in the United States and such figures as I have been able to dig up for Canada, suggest to me that something of the order of 40 per cent of our medical bills are already paid by various levels of government which include the three levels, namely federal, provincial and municipal. That figure includes what is being paid for the health care of Indians and Eskimos. It includes medical services for the armed forces and such medical services as are provided for veterans. It includes the health grants and includes the various services provided by the provinces and the municipalities. Hence we are on the way. Social medicine is not something new. Its first stages are here. The Canadian people accept the fact that the cost of medicine is a social responsibility. All we are asking is that we visualize the immense possibilities for the health of our people, both curative and preventive, in going ahead with this program on a vast scale.
Someone might ask why I make a speech like this at this time. Why not let the government hang back? Why not let the government fail? Why not let the government muff this matter? It just so happens, Mr. Speaker, that it does not matter to me who brings in a national health scheme. It does not matter to me who gets the credit for it. My concern is that something be done. For that reason I deliberately chose to make this speech today, so that I might do my best to prod the federal government representatives at that conference to take the kind of action that will see the early establishment in Canada of an over-all health insurance scheme which, right at the start, will provide diagnostic, laboratory and X-ray services as well as hospitalization and which, just as soon as possible, will provide

medical and dental services and out-of-work benefits to those who are unemployed because of illness.
A great many people will be involved in working out this scheme, including all the various levels of government and the medical profession. Once again I make my appeal to our friends the doctors in this country who have rendered tremendous service to the people of Canada over the years. One also recognizes the transition that they have had to go through as society's attitude toward these things has changed. I think most of us feel that it is unfortunate that doctors, who have such great capacity for doing a real job and adding to the health of our people, should be obliged to be concerned about economic matters and should have to put the question of making a living even alongside the question of the good they can do for Canadian human beings. I feel that any health insurance plan owes a great deal to the doctors and owes it to them to consider their position, but I also think that the doctors owe a great deal to the Canadian people and that it is their job to find ways of co-operating in a plan that will give the best possible services to all our people in this extremely important field.
There are two or three other subjects, Mr. Speaker, about which I should like to say a few words. First of all, I must say that I listened with interest to what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said on January 16, as reported first at page 124 of Hansard, at the beginning of his speech, and then at page 129 of Hansard, at the end of his speech. He said this:
The speech from the throne was brought down at a time when the Canadian economy is travelling in the highest possible gear.
That is the theme song of the Canadian government: things are rolling at top speed. Then at the end of his speech he said:
The attitude of the government is that it wants strength and progress through sufficiency.
I am prepared to accept that statement as a motto or as a goal. But in all seriousness I raise the question as to how those words, "strength and progress through sufficiency", fall on the ears of Canada's old age pensioners. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) may get to his feet as often as he wants to and decry the questions I ask about this matter. He may talk about the committee recommendation that was made in 1950. The fact of the matter is that, since the present figure of $40 a month was set, our gross national product has gone up by over 60 per cent. The gross national product in 1949, when the figure of $40 was set, was $16-4 billion. Estimates for 1955 put it at
The Address-Mr. Knowles $26-3 billion; that is an increase of 60-3 per cent. If the gross national product this year reaches $27 billion, as some economists are forecasting, that will represent an increase of 65 per cent over the gross national product of 1949.
I feel it is little enough to ask for, Mr. Speaker, that our old age pensioners should get a corresponding increase in the pension that is paid to them. A 65 per cent increase in the pension which is now $40 a month would bring it to $66 a month. In other words, those labour organizations that are asking for a pension of $65 a month, in my view, are right on the beam. I decry the attitude of the government that these questions should not be asked. I decry the attitude of the government that this matter was settled because there was a committee that made a report in 1950. I decry the attitude of the government that the job is all sewn up because the means test was eliminated. The fact of the matter is that time moves on. No piece of social legislation is perfect for all time. No piece of social legislation ends the story or ends the fight for social justice and a fair deal for the citizens of this land. I insist that the time has come at this session for action on the question of old age pensions. In my view the amount should be increased at least to that figure of $65 or $66 a month for those on old age security, for those on old age assistance and for those on blind persons allowances as well. If we accept that figure for these groups, I suggest the same figure should apply in the case of those on disability allowances. I want also to support the remarks made a few months ago by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) that something further should be done with regard to the War Veterans Allowance Act, particularly with respect to the question of the ceiling on permissible income.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has told us we are travelling in high gear; our economy is rolling full speed ahead. Economists tell us our gross national product is going to be larger than ever. To what avail, Mr. Speaker, this high gear, this tremendous gross national product, unless it gets through to our ordinary Canadian people in health and welfare and a decent standard of living, as well as those things that will make them feel that life is worth living in a country that has attained such progress as the government tells us we have accomplished.
I turn also for a moment to say a word on the question of housing. The government likes to boast of the number of new starts each year. I submit in all seriousness, Mr. Speaker, that the number of people who are
406	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Knowles losing their lives by fire in houses in this country should challenge this government to a tremendous speedup in its housing program. It is not enough just to be building new houses at high prices for people who can afford those high prices. A country whose economy is travelling in high gear, a country that feels it has great wealth, should be rebuilding from a quarter to half of the houses in this country or all those that are substandard and that continue to contain conditions that could result in further fires and a further loss of life. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, to what avail this high gear, this tremendous wealth, if thousands of our citizens must live in the kind of houses where life may be lost because of the danger of fire?
May I say a word now with respect to education. Here, too, I raise the same question. If we are travelling in high gear is it not a tragedy that in the field of education we seem to be slipping? I know the argument about education being a matter of provincial responsibility under the British North America Act. We in this group support that position taken in the British North America Act without question. The same situation holds in the United States, where education is a state responsibilty; yet President Eisenhower only recently recognized in a public statement that there comes a time when a matter such as education is of such importance to the nation as a whole that the nation as a whole has to consider the financial base upon which education is supported. I plead very strongly, Mr. Speaker, with this government to reconsider its position in this field, and to recognize the need for federal aid to education so that we can go ahead and not slip behind certain other areas of the world which are taking the lead over North America.
It has been suggested to me that there ,s one field where just a few million dollars -and that is easy for this government to find-could reverse the trend and that is in the matter of scientific training. We are not getting enough recruits in that field in order to keep pace with developments in the scientific world. We are losing many people to the country to the south of us. It has been suggested to me by experts in this field that just a few million dollars spent in scholarships could reverse the trend and keep Canada in the forefront in scientific training. The whole question of education is so important, so basic to our nation today and
[K-. Knowles.]

to our future, and of such nation-wide concern that I cannot but deplore the continued refusal of the government to concern itself with the financing of education. Once again I join my colleagues in this group and other members in other parties in the house; I join those groups of teachers, school trustees and municipal bodies who call upon this government for federal aid to education, without further delay.
I shall be through in a minute, Mr. Speaker, I accept the word of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that this nation's economy is in high gear, that this nation's economy is rolling ahead at full speed. I accept his assertion that strength and progress through sufficiency is a desirable goal. I call upon the government to put that assertion into practice. To what avail this high gear, if it is just statistics and figures and huge profits for large corporations? Let us get the benefit of this high gear, this fast rolling economy, this great sufficiency, through to our Canadian people. There are many ways in which it can be done. I have suggested some of them. I urge immediate action in the field of education, with respect to our veterans, in the field of housing, and in the matter of social security where the old age and blind pensions and pensions for disabled persons should be increased. Finally, I urge immediate action on the question I dealt with in the opening part of my remarks, a satisfactory national health plan. I urge that health insurance be brought in, and that it be based financially in such a way that it will get to our Canadian people, regardless of their individual financial capacity, the health services they need and which medical science is able to provide.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I join with previous speakers in offering my heartiest congratulations to the mover (Mrs. Shipley) and the seconder (Mr. Laflamme) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. With her customary grace, the hon. member for Timiskaming did splendidly in her description of the needs and geographical position of her constituency. She

told us, too, of its natural resources and we are grateful to her for giving us this information.
As for the seconder of the motion, though he is one of the younger members of this He explained the needs of his constituency and described, in a very clear fashion, what his constituency is like. Like the mover of the address, the hon. member for Bellechasse is certainly a valuable newcomer to this side of the house.
The people of those two constituencies are certainly proud of their members and, in any event, just by looking at the latter's smiling countenances, it could be assumed that their electors have decided to renew their mandate.
Mr. Speaker, I would very much like to say a few words of the fine constituency which I have the honour to represent, the constituency of Stanstead. As is well known, it is situated in the eastern townships, along the American border, from the state of Vermont to the city of Sherbrooke, which is aptly called the Queen of the eastern townships.
The population of Stanstead is mixed. It is mostly made up of French Canadians, with their love of hard work, joviality, and friendliness. But we have too some English-speaking Canadians, courteous and well versed in business matters, who are a great source of pride to us in that part of the country. To complete this picture of good understanding, we should also speak of those who live on the American border. A large number of those people who live across from us, on the far side of the border, share in our activities. This American element adds to this spirit of good neighbourliness of which we are so proud.
We should not overlook the part played by the Rotary Club and the chamber of commerce in the establishment of this policy of bonne entente in our area, a policy whereby we fraternize daily with our neighbours.
In fact, to illustrate what I say, I might point out that, on the occasion of the American Legion convention in Newport last year, an event to which all governors of New England states were invited, I had the great honour of being one of the guests, which afforded me the opportunity of meeting the governor of the state of New Hampshire, Mr. Dwinell, and the governor of the state of Vermont, Mr. Johnson, and to appreciate even more their spirit of bonne entente.
The Address-Mr. Roberge Hence, I am convinced that they will continue to co-operate as in the past. I take advantage of this opportunity to extend to them my best wishes for the new year.
Coming back to the American Legion convention, I must say that I was very proud to see the R.C.M.P. band supply the music on this occasion. On this, may I be permitted to thank the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) who kindly helped us to obtain permission to use this band, as well as the R. C. M. P. commissioner who granted our request. The presence of this band in Newport, besides being great publicity, brought great credit to Canada. Newspapers of the surrounding area, as well as those of the New England states, and all my fellow citizens talked about it for a long time. I also congratulate the members of this band for their dignified behaviour and for providing entertainment which was appreciated by all.
Mr. Speaker, I want to talk now about some geographical situations and, above all, of the industries of this constituency, large or small, in all their forms.
The Beebe district has a granite industry operating on a fairly large scale. As a matter of fact, the Sun Life building in Montreal is a monument to the credit of that little village. Thanks to the co-operation of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) and of my colleague the hon. member for Sherbrooke, the granite you will see in the public building of Sherbrooke was from Stanstead county; it goes without saying that I am proud of that fact because it is going to be a great help to our region as far as employment for our people and publicity for our products are concerned.
In my home town of Rock Island, we have a steel plant which makes precision tools for industry, heavy as well as light. They are tools used in the aircraft, automotive and mining industries, etc. That plant is quite busy. It employs some 600 people, and I am told it is constantly expanding. I heard recently that it had taken on a number of new workers, which is good news indeed for the future of our region.
In the western part of my county and looking towards Coaticook there is a very prosperous little town which makes such products as fire hose, wooden furniture, textile, nylon and rayon. I was told some time ago that these industries are comparatively stable, although I imagine that, like anywhere else,
408	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Roberge there is always room for improvement. At the present time people seem to be well satisfied.
If we turn northwards we come to Lennox-ville, which was formerly part of Sherbrooke county but which has been added to Stanstead county.
At the time of the redistribution, and lately during my first election campaign, I had my leg pulled about this beautiful town of Len-noxville; but I must assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I am very proud to have the town of Lennoxville among those of my county, for its people are generally of a practical mind and they made a jolly good town for themselves. There is an asbestos roofing industry, and a few lesser ones. Lennoxville also has a university, of which we are proud, Bishop's College, the graduates of which are a credit to this institution all over the country and in all the spheres of society. Our experimental farm, under the able management of Dr. Merrier, is doing a wonderful job for our locality and our farmers from the eastern townships also benefit from its activity. And I hope things will go on as before.
To go back to the west, we come to the town of Magog, largest in the county. Magog is connected with the larger centres by the Canadian Pacific Railway and, moreover, is crossed in east-westerly direction by a national highway. The town has a population of 11,000. It is, I think, very satisfied with present conditions, though a year or more ago, things did not look very bright, for the town to some extent is dependent upon the textile industry; the Dominion Textile Company indeed has one of its main factories in Magog.
About a month ago, the company's manager assured me that the situation was now rather satisfactory. I was happy to hear this, because last fall, the outlook was rather grim, and heavy clouds seemed to gather on the horizon. There were rumours of unemployment during the winter, and also of an impending strike.
Fortunately, just before the Christmas season, an agreement was reached and the strike was avoided. Winter, therefore, began under good auspices, and I take this opportunity to congratulate the members of the Catholic union for their foresight. As I was saying a while ago, friendly understanding prevails in our district. All concerned were called upon to show their good will, which 

went a long way towards avoiding the strike. I, therefore, congratulate their president, Mr. Victor Lamontagne, as well as the manager of Dominion Textile, Mr. Jeff Moynan, for their particular co-operation with regard to the settlement of the matter. The latter showed a great understanding .of both the company's interests and the workers' needs.
Now, the middle part of the constituency of Stanstead on the whole is rural. The future of agriculture having been discussed on many previous occasions, although I do not want to come back to the matter I feel I should point out that our farmers, as I stated before, live almost in a small paradise on earth. This earthly paradise, however, could still be improved. Some of our farmers are rather well organized as far as co-operatives and marketing are concerned.
In fact, towns close to the county provide them with a market for many of their products. In addition, they have access to a most favourable American market where they can sell their hay and cattle, although it is less interesting at the present time, for beef and other livestock sell at lower prices in the United States than on our own market, so that the prospects at the local level are good.
I believe, however, our farmers visualize the situation from a good angle. With their realistic approach, they anticipate better sales. For in our district the farmer must have a good business training to market his products. He must have also some know-how in mechanics, because in my county mechanization is gaining ground rapidly.
With his tractor and all the rest of his farm machinery the farmer must be enough of a mechanic to keep them operating. We can, in fact, see this every day; he is a good mechanic. Moreover the farmer must be content with a reasonable profit. True, he does receive more for his produce now than was formerly the case but this increase is not commensurate with the increased cost of the equipment he must buy to maintain his farm, etc. Still, he is not unreasonable and faces this situation with stoicism.
I should like to say to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that the farmers of our area are grateful to the present government which, through him, gives a great deal of assistance to agriculture through the maintenance of support prices on dairy products as well as of premiums on hogs, and

also through subsidies on transportation of lime.
And, on this matter of transportation of lime, farmers in the eastern townships, who are close to lime quarries, do not, in my opinion, fully appreciate this situation. They do not seem to be interested in taking advantage of this product, of which there is such a need in my area.
I believe that I have given a fairly exact description of the situation in my constituency, as I have availed myself of the latitude given us in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne to elaborate on several topics.
I should like, in passing, to express full support of my colleague from Sherbrooke (Mr. Gingues) as regards health insurance. I do not wish to elaborate on what he said. With his talent and foresight, he gave to the house a fine outline of health insurance and I do want to repeat that I support him unreservedly.
There is a further point I should like to deal with for the welfare of my district. It has to do with the construction of an airport and once more I join my colleague in supporting that idea. Last year steps were taken to that effect and the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) undertook to consider the project. I hope the study has advanced to a point where before long we may expect an announcement on the construction of an airport, in the vicinity of Sherbrooke.
Now, Mr. Speaker, our junior boards of trade in Coaticook and Magog have initiated a campaign this winter against the sale of obscene literature. I want to congratulate them on their move. They start their inquiry by looking over the books to be found on the stands and which, even though they are not too bad, are nothing but cowboy stories, murder stories and the like, and, as such, are not suitable reading for our young people. To my mind, it is important to consider that problem and to act before it is too late. But what is still more serious is the clandestine sale of certain books provided by special agents, books which lead to corruption, books that are obscene. As a matter of fact, I rather believe that the sex crime wave of which we have heard so much lately is connected with these disgusting and revolting books. An inquiry might show us that these criminals spent their idle hours wallowing in the reading of this obscene literature until, unable to control themselves, they attacked the first passer-by, the unhappy victim of these unbalanced people being quite often some poor little child.
The Address-Mr. Roberge
I would compare these people to the hyena which roams about the desert at night looking for putrefying corpses, because they like to wallow in filth, in all that is dirty. That is where they find their pleasure.
I know that that field is under municipal and provincial authorities. However, I would ask the Minister of Justice to take whatever steps he can so that the law will be complied with in so far as the sale of pornographic literature is concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to follow the example of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) and other hon. members who have spoken in both languages during this debate, and make a few observations in English. I think this would indicate our full belief in the bonne entente which our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) wants to bring into being. I think the use of both languages is completely in line with the procedure followed in this house.
I should like to deal with a matter which is a rather complex and touchy one. A few years ago I would not have dared to mention this, but conditions have changed and things are looking brighter all over the world. I refer to Japanese immigration. Everyone realizes that to deal with this problem a few years ago would have been out of the question, but the peace treaty has been signed and the Japanese have adopted our democratic way of life and perhaps it is our duty to try to keep them in that way of life.
Japan is not a member of the United Nations but recently she has shown a spirit of real co-operation. I do not want to put this in the way of a formal request but perhaps I could suggest to the minister of immigration that a change be made in our immigration laws. Under the present law Japanese immigrants are not permitted to enter this country; our doors are closed to them. I think under present conditions our minister of immigration might be permitted to remove this stigma from the Japanese people and open our doors a little.
As I have stated to the former minister of immigration, I do not believe in open-door immigration, but I like to see immigration treated realistically. People who are permitted to enter this country should be those who can comply with our immigration laws. We do not want all aristocrats and blue-blooded people, but those who come here must have good health, good character and have a good background. They must have everything that will help to make them good citizens.

The Address-Mr. Roberge Although the Japanese people are used to a different climate and have a different religion and way of life, I think they can become good citizens of Canada.
In the constituency of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Deslieres) there are some Japanese who were displaced persons during the war. They have assimilated themselves into the population of that district and have become good citizens. I have talked over this problem with some responsible people, one being a former member of parliament who has been to Japan a couple of times and has studied the problem over there. He tells me that when he goes there to do business he finds the Japanese willing to enter into negotiations for the exportation of goods or perhaps the purchase of some of our products, but during the course of conversations with them they always ask, "What have you Canadians against the Japanese that you will not permit immigration into your country?"
Our representatives over there are rather on the spot because they cannot reply to a question like that. All they can do is to reply the best they can. As I say, I have discussed this matter with Mr. Halle, a former member of parliament, and we may hear more about it later. He has told me that a change in our policy in this regard would help our export trade in the way of cattle and raw materials with some manufactured goods. He says that there is a good market in Japan for farm machinery. It would also help our commerce with Japan in other ways.
I know it will be said that if we open our doors we will have too many Japanese coming into the country, but that is something for the powers that be to decide. We are looking for markets all over the world and I think this would offer a chance to improve our situation in that direction. Our missionaries over there would be benefited in carrying our social welfare education. There is always this feeling in the minds of the Japanese and they treat our missionaries in an inferior way. They do not have the freedom that they would have otherwise. I hope the minister will give a little consideration to this problem.
As I said before, I am not in favour of open-door immigration, but it could be done on a strict quota basis. We should treat the Japanese the same as we do the people of other countries in that part of the world. This concludes what I have to say on the Japanese situation although I could extend my remarks and speak a little longer.
Another problem I should like to mention is one that has been mentioned before in
TMr. Roberge.1

this house, though I do not think it has ever been very much discussed. Although I do not wish to labour the matter, I just want to say a few words on what is called the world calendar.
In our days, speed prevails in our way of living, and everything is streamlined in industry, in accounting, in manufacturing processes and in everything connected with industry and trade. This world calendar would meet present conditions better than the Gregorian calendar we are now using. I have nothing against the present calendar, but as we have improved many things in our way of living, this is just one suggestion that I place before the house.
Most of the industrial people and religious people with whom I have talked over this matter have no great objection to it. However, it has to be adopted on the higher level, and I would leave the problem to the Canadian standards association or to the cabinet to be presented. I believe the only way it could be adopted would be by the United Nations.
The purpose of this world calendar would be to improve, regularize and stabilize our time system. I believe it would more adequately meet our modern conditions and would respond more to the present needs of industry, government, agriculture, religion, science and education-every field, one might say.
I shall not describe this calendar at length, as many of you have probably read about it. It has only a few alterations as compared with the present calendar. The quarters would begin on the 1st of January, 1st of April, 1st of July and 1st of October. In those months there would be 31 days, and all the other months would have 30 days, but at the end of the year a day would be added which would be a world holiday. The advantage of this calendar is that it would be permanent. We would not have to get one every year. It would be the same year after year. If you were planning future engagements of any kind, you would know, for instance, that if the 5th of May this year falls on Sunday, the 5th of May would fall on Sunday every year thereafter.
Mr. Speaker, in order that members may have a better idea of this calendar, would I be permitted to place it on record on Hansard as an appendix?

However, I noticed that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) spent one and a half hours talking about it, saying that there was nothing in the speech from the throne and so on. We have had statements from banks and commercial interests that 1955 was an outstanding year, one of the best years we ever had, and they are looking forward to 1956 being another good year. With all these accomplishments the government certainly deserves great credit; but every Canadian throughout the country has also contributed to this state of affairs, otherwise it would not be so. If every Canadian farmer stays at his plough, every machinist in the shops stays at his machine and every banker stays at his desk throughout the whole economy of the country, then 1956 will be even better than 1955. The same applies to 1957, and I think that in 1957 we shall see another glorious year for the Liberal party.
